observations: A teal figure with a rounded, oversized head stands upright against a dark grey background; broad flat shapes with dark outlines separate limbs from torso.

A jagged zigzag crown of teal lines rises from the top of the head; a small red circular scribble sits on the upper left of the face, and a second cluster of red zigzag marks appears at the right jaw.
Two long thin teal lines trail downward from the figure's right side, while the left arm extends outward ending in a flattened open hand shape.
reading: Teal fills the figure almost uniformly, making it read as a single flat shape punched from the dark grey field. The jagged crown lifts the silhouette into something alert or bristling; two small red marks—one wound tight at the forehead, one frantic at the jaw—concentrate attention on the face and can read as points of pressure or distress. Trailing lines at the right side lend a sense of unfinished motion, as though something is still being shed.
contextAngle: Within the owned nnotb subset, this work sits between title neighbors #265 and #267. All three share an upright figure and jagged crown, but each uses a distinct background color and line weight, making the crown a recurring mark rather than a fixed symbol.

connections.reason: nnxyz nnotb #265 shares the same jagged-crown silhouette and upright stance but uses pink-on-black instead of teal-on-dark grey, and places its circular mark at the eye rather than the forehead.

nnxyz nnotb #267 carries a red spiral mark overlaid on a head form, allowing direct comparison of how the same red-circle device functions across two very different color fields and figure treatments.

lookingQuestion: Where do the two red marks sit in relation to the figure's outline, and how does their placement change what you look at first?
ambiguities: The two trailing teal lines at the figure's right side are ambiguous—they could read as hair, a cape, or detached limbs.
nnxyz nifty faces #23 was inspected but omitted: its dense multicolor line-fill and absence of a figure silhouette offer no useful formal connection to this work.
